All I do know is that when he finishes I shall have to decide as between using time to cross-examine on the matters that he's dealt with already or on other matters, and I haven't made any decisions on that. It's entirely conceivable that cross-examination on some of the matters that he's raised today simply I won't be ready for them tomorrow because I won't be in a position to take a position, so I might find myself asking for adjournment of, in any event, part of the cross-examination. I very much hope not, but I just raise it as a possibility so that if the accused forecasts finishing with this witness early tomorrow, he and those advising him might need to have another witness available for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We have another matter tomorrow as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I forgot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there really anything in what we've heard today that requires cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, there may well be not, Your Honour, but in any case, I'm just explaining that that would, of course, be another reason for the accused having another witness here. One way and another, I'd ask him to have that in mind, because last week we lost an entire session for lack of witness availability, or lack of witness readiness. I don't know against whose account that is being counted but it would be very unfortunate if it happened again tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll bear that in mind, Mr. Nice. It's now time for the adjournment. We could spend another five minutes. Another five minutes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For instance, Mr. Robinson, just one key point: In 63(e), it says that a number of people were shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, is it the case that here in tab 1.4 we have a chronological list of all incidents involving loss of life, even if a person died in a hospital?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we can find that under that tab.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we see, for instance, from number 113, under number 113, even though it's not translated, we can see the number and the date. That's where the 24th March begins, and then it goes on. Let us see, since we have the 27th, the 28th, and other dates here, we can see that on the 27th a member of the army of Yugoslavia was killed, Srdjan, son of Radmilo, Milosevic. It says on the 27th of March, one soldier killed. On the 28th -- the previous incident I mentioned was in Klina, not in Pec. In Istok on the 28th, another Serb was killed, Bratislav Radnic. In Celopek, near Pec, on the 30th of March, Milos Otovic, Veljko Petrovic, member of the army, was killed in Kapusnica [phoen]. On the 31st of March two persons killed; Dragan Makic and Sladjan Stosic, lieutenant. A number of people with less serious injuries. Serbs. The first Albanian casualty is on the 1st of April. Adem Seljmaj, killed from a small calibre gun. His wife, Rahima Gashi, a civilian. It goes on to mention the criminal report made, et cetera. A common law marriage was involved in this case. And then again on the 1st of April another policeman was killed, Igor Urosevic. 1st of April another Serbian casualty. On the 2nd of April, Serbian casualty, and so on. And only on the 2nd of April in Pec, in the settlement of Kakaric, a member of the KLA, Ahmet Hasani, from Pec, was killed. As we can see from here, this was the first person killed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thus, if it says in the indictment that on the 27th and 28th March, 1999, a number of people were shot by the army and the police, would then somebody be killed in Pec in those days if the army and the police were shooting?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did anyone get killed in Pec during those days? We have the documentation here.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of anyone who fired a gun in Pec in those first days when the bombing began, when people were fleeing Pec?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I have no such information. Maybe there was some sporadic shooting, but not targeted shooting at specific persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we see from these documents that nobody was killed. Do you remember any shooting?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult for me to say whether there was any shooting on that day in particular because there was shooting all the time. We're talking about a plane here. Any shooting is heard at several kilometres distance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in these particular days quoted here, can you tell us that nobody got hurt?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it says here that a number of people were shot. It says so in the indictment, and we can establish whether they were or they were not. It also says that houses were set on fire. Did anyone from the army or the police set a single house on fire in Pec?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: No. Neither the police nor the army ever did anything of the kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any fires in Pec at the time? And let us be precise: We are talking about the 27th and the 28th of March when great masses of people were gathering in the centre of Pec town. Were there any fires?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes, there were fires.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Somewhere on the outskirts. You could see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Did fire brigades intervene?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't they?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Well, they were unable to go there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were they unable; for security reasons or --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: What do you mean why? The moment we moved to go anywhere, we get shot at. How can we send fire brigades? Fire brigades are not members of the SUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All fire brigades, as we know, are parts of the Ministry of the Interior. If the fire brigades were unable to go to those areas where there were fires because they were shot at the moment they tried, was anyone able to go there to set a house on fire in those areas controlled by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Nobody from our side could do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, there are about five other allegations in 65(e). You can just go through them in the seven remaining minutes before 2.00 and close your examination of this witness. That would be a very good use of the time. He's from Pec, and he can testify as to these allegations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let us deal with all the allegations. We have dealt with the shooting. There were no casualties among Albanians, no wounded, no killed. We have dealt with arsons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm looking at all the allegations here. Are you aware that policemen and soldiers were deployed in every street and forcing Kosovo Albanians to leave?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: There were no soldiers deployed. Policemen were deployed but not in every street. They were deployed in intersections where they performed their regular job, but there were no troops, no army troops around.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But the deportation allegation, that they were forcing people to go to the town centre and then, once there, forced them to get on buses and being driven to Prizren, can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is precisely what I was going to ask him. Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regarding the deployment of the police, we have clarified that there was no army, whereas the police occupied its normal posts to regulate traffic.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many policemen were there on that day in the centre of Pec, in total, where they performed their regular jobs?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I don't know about that day. I can tell you the total number --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us the maximum possible number of policemen that could have been present in the broader centre of Pec.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: There could have been no more than 50 in total in the broader centre, depending on what you call the broader centre. We had certain permanent police posts that were always manned by the police to control movement of vehicles and persons. We had certain restrictions. We could not man more posts even if we had wanted to. We work in four or five shifts. We have a certain available number of policemen that we divide into four or five shifts, and that's all we can do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were occupying their regular police posts.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We clarified this. Now, tell me, do you know whether anyone forced Albanians to board buses or trucks in order to leave Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: No. Why buses or trucks? They could move around any way they pleased. They could go in their own carts, in their own cars, in their ox carts, in tractors. Why would anybody force them onto buses?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just pointing to this sentence from 63(e) which says, "Once the people reached the centre of town, those without cars or vehicles were forced to get on buses or trucks and were driven to the town of Prizren." I have quoted to you this entire sentence. Tell me, is this true or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: First of all, it doesn't make sense to me. It seems to say that these people first arrived into the centre of town and then those who did not have cars were forced to board buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you now referring to what I just quoted? Is that true or not true?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I don't even understand what is meant by this allegation. So in order for this to be true, somebody was standing in the centre of town to establish who had a car and who didn't. If you had a car, you could go on and if you didn't have a car, you had to go onto the bus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you know or did you hear of Albanians getting on buses and trucks and getting out of the town of -- and getting out of the town and moving -- and going on to Prizren?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I neither saw nor heard anybody boarding buses, but I heard that people left by bus. People left in their own passenger cars, in their ox carts, tractors, buses as well. I haven't heard of anybody who left by truck, but that also is possible because I wouldn't have been able to see anybody under a tarpaulin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please. There is one question that is critical here: Did anyone force an Albanian to board a bus in order to leave?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I know nothing about that. I never heard or saw anything of the kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said there was no army around. Was any policeman performing the job of forcing Albanians to board buses in order to leave?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Well, the police was regulating traffic and performing all the other normal police work; protecting lives, protecting property, but that did not include putting people on buses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where exactly were you on the 27th and 28th of March?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was probably the day when the centre of Pec was so terribly overcrowded. On that day, I was in the centre of Pec, and I was moving along other roads. There were bottlenecks. During those days, I even went to Kula, which is a pass leading to Montenegro. All the streets were completed flooded with people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What were you doing on those days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was giving instructions to the traffic police to take up posts in a certain place, to accelerate the movement of vehicles. For instance, in the control post at Savine Vode, I told policemen to simplify the procedure of control to let a maximum number of vehicles through towards Kula, because this is an uphill road. Movement is very slow. So if you stop a vehicle --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we're coming -- I want you could conclude your examination-in-chief, and then tomorrow or the next day that we meet we'll deal with the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have quite a number of questions left to ask this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... of this witness's testimony, and I will only allow you to ask any further questions if they are relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: For another three minutes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. To make this absolutely precise, at the time you were chief of traffic police.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You regulated traffic as usual?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The only difference is when there are more crowds and when there are less.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes. And then we try to divert traffic to different directions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know about gatherings of Albanians in the centre of Pec and their departure?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I'm trying to remember that precise date, but I know that during those days there were intense crowds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were in a particular place yourself. Where did the citizens gather?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: On the square in the centre of Pec.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: From various parts of the town and from villages. That's what I know from reports from my patrols.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many civilians were there in the centre?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: The square was full. In my own estimate, there were about 10.000 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone address the citizens?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: I do not know the Albanian language. There were some speeches made. I don't know what those people were saying. I don't know even who they were. This was not an organised rally so that we would know from an announcement who was going to hold speeches. There were some shouts and speeches through the bullhorn, but I don't know what was being said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was unofficial talk between them, but did any authorities address them?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: No. There were no authorities present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any citizens address you personally?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they ask you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: They were questions that I couldn't understand even at the time, but I later understood what they meant. They asked me whether they could go to Montenegro in their own cars. I couldn't understand why on earth they were asking me that. I told them simply that they were free to go wherever they pleased and using whatever vehicle they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. They asked you whether they could take cars to Montenegro and go to Montenegro by car and you said that they could go wherever they wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK
utterances.text: Yes. They were asking whether the police or the military would prevent them from doing so, and our answer was that no one would restrict them in any way, either if they wanted to move towards Montenegro or other parts of the country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, please --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have to stop now. We have gone 20 minutes beyond the break. There is another matter that the Chamber will be hearing tomorrow, but the parties should be on standby for the resumption of this case in the event that that becomes possible. I hope that is clear. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to ask something. Do you have something different going on tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we do. Yes. But you have to be on standby in the event that that matter concludes in sufficient time for us to continue this hearing. And the Registry will take care of logistical arrangements.
